channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Junk food affects cognition and mental health, study finds
item.description: A new study led by Flinders University has shed light on how poor dietary choices in childhood and adolescence can contribute to mental health and cognitive problems and potentially other diseases.

item.title: DNA differences shape how cells respond to alcohol, nicotine and caffeine
item.description: A new study from the University of Chicago and Johns Hopkins University maps gene-by-environment interactions across many cell types in response to common exposures like alcohol, nicotine and caffeine. In the future, researchers hope to use such interactions to predict how environmental factors will affect an individual person.

item.title: Physical activity prepares the brain for psychotherapy in the treatment of depression
item.description: A new study shows that regular physical exercise can enhance the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for mild to moderate depression. The international clinical trial, published in the journal Mental Health and Physical Activity, demonstrated that 12 weeks of prior training improved patients' cardiorespiratory fitness, resulting in significant gains in memory and learning during the psychotherapy phase.

item.title: What is a CAC test, and should you get one?
item.description: A coronary artery calcium, or CAC, test is a quick, noninvasive CT scan that looks for calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can be an early sign of plaque buildup, or atherosclerosis. The resulting "calcium score" can give individuals and their health care professionals another piece of information about future risk of cardiovascular disease or an event such as a heart attack or stroke.

item.title: New approach aims to make treatment more accessible for children with rare brain disorders
item.description: McGill University researchers have developed and tested a new way to facilitate the creation of personalized genetic therapies for children with rare neurodevelopmental disorders. Currently, many children suffering from rare disorders are left without a realistic path to treatment, given that the underlying genetic changes may affect only a handful of patients. As such, there is a need for platforms that treat diagnosis as the starting point for therapeutic evaluation rather than the endpoint of a diagnostic journey.

item.title: More medical data needs more shared understanding
item.description: The shift from paper documents to electronic health records (EHRs) in health care has taken decades. Thanks to federal incentive payments for digitizing records, nine out of 10 doctors' offices were using EHRs by 2021. But clinics and hospitals are still figuring out how to use them to improve patient outcomes. New research from the McCombs School of Business at The University of Texas at Austin can give them some fresh ideas.

item.title: Cold hard facts: When ice baths help... and when they hurt
item.description: A major review has found that plunging into cold water after exercise can speed recovery and boost performance in some situations—but using it after every workout could be detrimental to strength and muscle gains.

item.title: Injured e-scooter riders face higher risk of serious head or neck trauma than injured cyclists
item.description: Adults injured while riding e-scooters had a higher risk of serious head or neck injury than those injured on bicycles, even though their injuries were less severe overall, according to a national trauma-center analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons (JACS). Injured e-bike and bicycle riders, meanwhile, had similar risks of severe or critical injury after researchers accounted for differences in rider and crash characteristics.

item.title: Semaglutide may improve eating disorder symptoms and body image in adults seeking obesity treatment
item.description: Adults receiving semaglutide for obesity treatment experienced greater improvements in several measures of disordered eating, eating disorder symptoms and body image concerns compared with participants receiving placebo, according to a new study led by researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The study was published in the International Journal of Eating Disorders.

item.title: Study finds some BRCA2 gene changes carry lower breast cancer risk
item.description: Mayo Clinic researchers, in a study published in Nature Communications, have identified a group of BRCA2 gene variants associated with a moderate risk of breast cancer, a finding that could help health care teams better assess a person's cancer risk and personalize care.

item.title: Urgent action needed to safeguard the effectiveness of antibiotics
item.description: With mounting evidence that antibiotic-resistant bacteria are continuing to spread and treatment options are becoming increasingly limited, urgent action is needed to safeguard the effectiveness of antibiotics, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on the occasion of European Antibiotic Awareness Day.

item.title: Mild Alzheimer's patients benefit from 40Hz sensory stimulation in national clinical trial
item.description: At the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston Nov. 16, MIT spinoff company Cognito Therapeutics announced the results of its pivotal clinical trial of a noninvasive, device-based approach to Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment first discovered in The Picower Institute in 2014. The "HOPE" trial included 663 people in two "prespecified" subgroups of volunteers: those with diagnoses of mild Alzheimer's and those with moderate Alzheimer's.

item.title: 'Perfectionist' as a label: Who claims it and who doesn't
item.description: It's a label people casually toss around in conversations about school, work and life in general: "perfectionist." But do young adults who call themselves perfectionists exhibit the behaviors and psychological traits associated with perfectionism?

item.title: New study offers clues to how young neurons may help the brain form social memories
item.description: How does the brain remember someone we have met before, especially when new and similar experiences compete for our attention?

item.title: Inspired by 'Flowers for Algernon,' experimental nose drops improve memory in mice
item.description: Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed experimental nose drops that enhance learning and memory in aged mice while also preventing memory loss in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The treatment uses mRNA technology similar to that developed for use in COVID-19 vaccines.

item.title: Chewable fish oil emulsion supplements may be better than soft-gel capsules
item.description: In a crossover clinical trial published in the European Journal of Lipid Science and Technology, investigators found that a chewable fish oil emulsion supplement may provide higher circulating levels of omega-3 fatty acids compared with a soft gel.

item.title: Multiple short walks better than one long walk for controlling blood sugar
item.description: A randomized trial published in Obesity indicates that interrupting prolonged sitting with frequent brisk walks can improve blood glucose regulation to a greater extent than the same amount of walking performed as a single continuous bout.

item.title: Nearly half of Australian health courses fail to mention sex and gender differences
item.description: Nearly half of Australia's accredited health and medical degrees do not mention sex or gender in a single course unit, according to a national review by the Center for Sex and Gender Equity in Health and Medicine at The George Institute for Global Health, despite extensive evidence that many conditions present differently in women, men and gender-diverse people.

item.title: Medicare boost needed for Australia's 1.6 million cancer survivors
item.description: More than 1.6 million Australians living with and beyond cancer could benefit from proposed Medicare reforms to increase subsidized allied health visits, a move backed by new Flinders University–led research.

item.title: Fingertip study reveals pain threshold during millimeter-wave exposure
item.description: Wireless technologies using millimeter waves are becoming increasingly important for high-speed communication, but their effects on human health need to be better understood. Heating of the skin is a well-established effect of exposure at these frequencies, yet the temperature at which people begin to experience pain remains uncertain. Previous studies using different heat sources have reported varying pain thresholds, while evidence from direct millimeter-wave exposure in highly sensitive areas, such as the fingertip, has been limited. Understanding when sensations progress from warmth to pain could help inform safer exposure guidelines.

item.title: Psilocybin may improve a difficult-to-treat symptom of depression, study finds
item.description: New research from the University of Colorado Anschutz suggests that psilocybin may help improve anhedonia, the loss of interest or ability to experience pleasure, in people with treatment-resistant depression. In a clinical trial, researchers found significant improvement in this difficult-to-treat symptom eight weeks after treatment, offering new insight into psilocybin's potential role in depression care.

item.title: Understanding epilepsy and seizures: Q&A with epileptologist
item.description: Epilepsy, a chronic neurological condition of the central nervous system, affects millions of people, with overactive or misfiring electrical signals in the brain leading to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.

item.title: FDA approves first factor XIa inhibitor for secondary stroke prevention
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Sunharbo (asundexian) 50 mg tablets, in combination with antiplatelet therapy, to reduce the risk for stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA).

item.title: New review protocol outlines plan to evaluate quit-smoking support for ADHD and autism
item.description: Published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the protocol "Smoking cessation interventions in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD)" was developed by the South East Smokefree Alliance in collaboration with academics at the University of Bristol.

item.title: Nearly 1 in 10 US adults report having chronic hand eczema
item.description: Chronic hand eczema (CHE) is common, impacting nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: FDA approves new drug for advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Janssen Biotech's Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed during or after receipt of platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

item.title: Paintball-related eye injuries declined 84.5% from 2005 to 2025
item.description: Paintball-related ocular injuries seen at U.S. emergency departments declined by 84.5% from 2005 to 2025, according to a research letter published online Nov. 5 in JAMA Ophthalmology.

item.title: Defibrillator drones could arrive ahead of ambulances in hundreds of cardiac arrest cases
item.description: Drones carrying defibrillators could arrive ahead of ambulances at hundreds of cardiac arrest incidents each year, potentially creating opportunities for earlier treatment, according to new research. The study, published in the journal Reliability Engineering & System Safety, also found they could improve emergency response coverage in parts of Scotland.

item.title: Family doctor shortage spurs new models of care
item.description: Dr. Aaron Block graduated from medical school carrying a quarter-million dollars of medical debt and got hired as a family medicine doctor for a health network.

item.title: Beer, but not wine, linked to higher risk of kidney injury
item.description: Regular drinkers of beer or spirits may face a significantly greater risk of acute kidney injury, according to a new study that analyzed data from more than 250,000 U.K. adults. However, the same association was not found for wine drinkers.
